questions.question: Explain three ways in which desert plants are adapted to survive with little water.
questions.expected_answer: Many desert plants store water in thick, juicy leaves, stems or trunks, such as succulents, aloes, the quiver tree and cacti. They find water with shallow roots that spread wide to soak up rain or with very long roots, like the camel thorn tree, that reach deep underground. They save water with small leaves, spines instead of leaves and a thick, waxy skin, and some survive dry years as seeds that sprout after rain.

questions.question: Describe two special desert plants.
questions.expected_answer: The welwitschia grows only in the Namib Desert and has just two long, leathery leaves that keep growing for its whole life, and some are thought to be many hundreds of years old. The quiver tree of Namaqualand and southern Namibia is a giant aloe that stores water in its trunk and branches and has a pale surface to reflect heat; the San are said to have made arrow quivers from its branches.

questions.question: Explain how three desert animals are adapted to survive.
questions.expected_answer: The camel can go many days without drinking, stores fat in its hump for energy, has wide feet for sand and long eyelashes and closable nostrils against blowing sand. The fennec fox has huge ears that give off heat and help it hear prey. The male sandgrouse carries water to its chicks in soaked belly feathers. Many desert animals are also nocturnal, sheltering in burrows during the hot day.
